title: Judge Gives Final Approval to Anthropic's $1.5 Billion Copyright Settlement, the Largest in U.S. History
excerpt: A federal judge in San Francisco signed off on the landmark deal resolving a class-action lawsuit by authors who accused Anthropic of using pirated books to train its Claude chatbot.
body:
• U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin granted final approval to Anthropic's $1.5 billion settlement, the largest known copyright recovery in U.S. history.
  • The class-action lawsuit accused the Amazon- and Alphabet-backed AI company of downloading more than 480,000 pirated books from shadow libraries to train its Claude chatbot.
  • Authors filed claims covering over 92% of the works in the settlement, with each book valued at approximately $3,000.
  • The ruling is the first major resolution among dozens of copyright cases against AI companies, potentially setting a benchmark for pending suits against OpenAI, Meta and others.

A federal judge in San Francisco on Monday gave final approval to Anthropic's $1.5 billion settlement of a class-action copyright lawsuit, closing the first major legal challenge to an AI company's use of copyrighted material for training and establishing what attorneys called the largest copyright recovery in American history.

U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin signed off on the deal, rejecting objections from authors who argued the payout was too small. The settlement resolves claims brought by a group of writers who accused Anthropic of downloading pirated versions of their books from shadow libraries Library Genesis and Pirate Library Mirror to train Claude, the company's AI chatbot.

How the Case Unfolded

The authors sued Anthropic in 2024, arguing the company — which is backed by Amazon and Alphabet — used pirated copies of their books without permission to teach Claude to respond to human prompts. The case moved quickly through the courts, producing a split ruling last June from now-retired Judge William Alsup.

"But the judge simultaneously ruled that the company violated authors' rights by saving more than seven million pirated books to a "central library" that would not necessarily be used for AI training."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=sDCnr3A5EPY

Alsup found that Anthropic's use of copyrighted works to train Claude constituted fair use, a significant win for the AI industry. But the judge simultaneously ruled that the company violated authors' rights by saving more than seven million pirated books to a "central library" that would not necessarily be used for AI training. A trial had been set for December to determine damages, with potential liability running into the hundreds of billions of dollars.

Facing what Anthropic described in court filings as "inordinate pressure," the company struck a deal in August. The settlement values each of the approximately 482,460 books at roughly $3,000, and requires Anthropic to destroy the datasets containing the pirated material.

"We are gratified by the Court's ruling granting final approval of this historic settlement. It is the largest known copyright recovery in history."

— Justin Nelson, Lead Attorney for the Authors

Objections Overruled

The settlement drew opposition from some authors who argued it was too small, overcompensated the plaintiffs' attorneys or wrongly excluded certain copyright owners. Judge Martinez-Olguin rejected each objection, writing that complaints about the settlement's size were "not grounded in a realistic assessment of the overall risks and rewards of a trial." The court awarded the attorneys more than $101 million of the $187.5 million they requested in fees.

Authors and other copyright holders filed claims covering over 92 percent of the works included in the settlement, according to the plaintiffs' attorneys. Some authors and publishers chose to opt out and have filed separate lawsuits against Anthropic that remain pending.

A Benchmark for the AI Industry

The case is one of dozens brought by copyright owners — including authors, news outlets and visual artists — against technology companies over the training of their large language models. It is the first major U.S. case to reach a resolution, making it a potential benchmark for pending suits against OpenAI, Meta, Midjourney and others.

The Association of American Publishers called the settlement "a major step in the right direction in holding AI developers accountable," while the Authors Guild expressed hope it would prompt other companies to respect copyright law in training their models.

For the broader AI industry, the mixed legal outcome — fair use for training, but liability for hoarding pirated material — offers both reassurance and warning. Companies that train on copyrighted content may have legal cover, but those that accumulate pirated datasets face significant exposure.
